doc.title: Joseph Daley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 18, 2018

title: Knowing how a spontaneous piece ends
summary: Endings arise like a conversation; last night's conflict over stopping time.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I had an interesting thing yesterday because I got to ask Warren how do you as a trio know when to end some of these spontaneous compositions. And then I got to see it last night, and hear it, that it sort of made sense. I can’t tell you why but it sounded like, I mean no one did a cut-off but it was sort of like —

If anybody does a cut-off we’re not going to look anyway. No the thing is it’s just like I’m talking to you and you’re talking to me. That’s the thing about, we’re talking to each other. You know when the conversation’s over you’re not going to cut me off and say the conversation’s over. The conversation just naturally just comes to an end. We talked about certain things and you will make a statement saying, you know, okay well thank you very much, and then I know automatically, oh it’s coming to an end. Well the same type of thing, you know, Warren will do something or Scott will do something or I’ll do something and then we’ll know, because you know last night, I don’t know if you — I’m going to talk to Scott about this tonight, I mean when we were driving in. But somebody told him that we had to end at a certain time.
And I heard in his playing that he was trying to make the ensemble stop. I heard it him pushing to that last note to get us to stop, because he wanted to stop at a certain time. But
I didn’t want to stop. That’s what I’m saying. Sometimes you have these conflicts. I didn’t want to stop because he told us that we could go —
